evidence.note: J'accuse! is a French production; France has been a Berne Convention member since 1887. Under 17 U.S.C. Â§ 104A (URAA, effective January 1, 1996), copyright could have been restored if the work entered US public domain due to formality failure â€” e.g., no US registration on the 1921 United Artists release, or failure to renew a registered copyright in the 1946â€“1949 window. However, even a fully restored URAA copyright receives only the remainder of the 95-year US copyright term measured from first publication. With first publication in 1919, that remainder expired January 1, 2015; reckoned from the 1921 US release date, January 1, 2017. Either calculation places the work firmly in the public domain as of 2026. URAA restoration provides no ongoing protection for a film of this vintage.

evidence.note: J'accuse! (1919) is a silent film released without a fixed recorded score; the underlying silent print is in the public domain. The 2007/2008 Lobster Films restoration (distributed on DVD by Flicker Alley) includes a new orchestral score composed by Robert Israel, which is an independently copyrighted work. Copies of this film in widespread circulation â€” including many online streams â€” frequently carry that score or other modern accompaniments. Any copy embedding music should be treated as potentially incorporating a protected composition or sound recording until the source is confirmed.

evidence.note: The story and screenplay were written by Abel Gance as an original work conceived for this film â€” no source novel, play, or prior published literary text has been identified as its basis. Note: Abel Gance's 1938 remake J'accuse! is a separate copyright and is not at issue here.

editorial:
J'accuse! is Abel Gance's 1919 anti-war epic produced by PathÃ© FrÃ¨res, built around a love triangle between two men conscripted into World War I. Its climactic 'return of the dead' sequence â€” in which fallen soldiers rise from their graves to demand that the living justify the carnage â€” was filmed using actual French poilus on brief leave from the front; Gance later said most were dead within weeks of the shoot. D.W. Griffith attended a private New York screening in 1921, was deeply moved, and arranged US distribution through United Artists under the title I Accuse, with a happy ending grafted on to suit American audiences.

The 1919 silent print is in the US public domain: the full 95-year copyright term ran from 1919 and expired January 1, 2015, and even a hypothetical URAA restoration of a lapsed foreign copyright would have expired by the same date. The rights trap is the 2007/2008 Lobster Films restoration, assembled by the Nederlands Filmmuseum from six archival sources including a reel of original camera negative and the only surviving tinted print, then released by Flicker Alley on DVD. That restoration and its Robert Israel orchestral score carry independent copyrights. Creators must source an unrestored print â€” the Internet Archive copy at archive.org/details/j-accuse.-1919 is confirmed as such â€” rather than rip the Flicker Alley disc.
faq: Can I use this film in a commercial project or YouTube video?

The 1919 silent print is in the US public domain â€” all copyright terms expired by January 1, 2015 at the latest. The trap is which copy you use: the 2007/2008 Lobster Films restoration sold by Flicker Alley on DVD is independently copyrighted, and the Robert Israel score embedded in it is protected separately. Download the unrestored print from Internet Archive (archive.org/details/j-accuse.-1919) rather than sourcing from the commercial disc.
Is the musical accompaniment on this film public domain?

The 1919 release was silent â€” there is no original sound track. The score most people encounter with modern copies is Robert Israel's orchestral composition written for the 2007 Lobster Films restoration; that piece is under copyright. To use the film with music, either present it silently, license a score separately, or commission your own accompaniment.
